quiz: Before coding anything, make sure you and the interviewer agree on what to build and what to skip.
Look for the noun that has its own data and lifecycle in the system.
If types differ only in data, not behaviour, a simple data-carrying type may be enough.
Think about global state, testability, and whether there could ever be more than one lot.
Both gates looked for a free spot, then claimed it. Ask whether those two steps run as one unit.
Make sure the ticket cannot be used twice and the spot is freed only after billing is done.
Per started hour means any partial hour counts as a full one. Round 61 minutes up to hours.
Each counter sums plus and minus ones along its line. When does a line belong entirely to one player?
Check the centre against each line rule: same row, same column, r equals c, and r plus c equals n minus 1.
Ask how to add a new kind of player without editing the Game class. Think of the Open/Closed principle.
Rules must stack on any tariff in any combination. Which pattern adds behaviour by wrapping the same interface?
Interviews test how well your design handles change, not just correct output.
Undo must restore exactly what execute changed, so all state must be updated consistently.
interview: Mention clarifying requirements, core entities, relationships, key APIs, patterns, code, and then handling extensions.
Ask about vehicle and spot types, floors, entry and exit gates, pricing, payments, concurrency, and what is out of scope.
Explain how follow-up changes break one big class, and how clear responsibilities and invariants make change safe.
Name each pattern, such as strategy for pricing or allocation, and tie it to a concrete change it supports.
Discuss atomic claim of a spot, locks or compare-and-set, and keeping the critical section small.
Cover ticket states, fee calculation on exit, payment handling, and preventing reuse of a closed ticket.
Explain row, column and diagonal counters updated per move, and why reaching n means a full line for one player.
Separate board, players, game rules and win checking, and explain what each class owns.
Introduce move commands with execute and undo, two stacks, and correct counter rollback.
Show adding a new spot type and a pricing rule through existing extension points with minimal edits.
Discuss per-floor or sharded allocation, fast free-spot lookups, concurrency, and persistence.
Put interfaces where variation is real or expected, and keep simple stable parts concrete.
Talk about cutting scope to get a working core, communicating with the interviewer, then improving.
